title: The earth
hook: Francis calls the earth sister and mother (Canticle of the Creatures)

segments.voice: Yesterday, loving animals. Your line was sister birds. Was one creature treated gently on purpose? Today, Francis again, and the ground under every one of those birds. Day eight hundred sixty-six.

Brother Sun. Sister Moon. Brother Wind. Sister Water. Brother Fire. That's the cast list of a short song by Francis of Assisi, the Canticle of the Creatures. Tradition says he made it late in his life, when he was sick and his eyes were failing: a song in praise of the sun, from a man who could hardly see it. He goes through the whole family of creation, one relative at a time. And then he reaches the ground under everyone's feet, and gives it two names at once. Today: what he called the earth, and three other old voices standing on the same soil.
screen: `BROTHER SUN, SISTER MOON.` → `A WHOLE FAMILY OF CREATION.` → `TWO NAMES FOR THE GROUND.`

segments.voice: First, brother sun, sister water. In the Canticle, Francis praises God through each creature, and he gives each one a family name. The sun is a brother, beautiful and radiant. Water is a sister, useful, humble, precious and pure. The point isn't decoration: in this song, the singer stands among the creatures as kin, not above them as owner. Second, our sister, mother earth. When Francis reaches the earth, one family word isn't enough. She's our sister, and she's our mother, who sustains us, governs us, and brings forth fruits and colored flowers and herbs. Sister: kin, alongside us. Mother: she feeds us. Third, to dress it and to keep it. Francis didn't invent this care. In Genesis, the first human is put in the garden of Eden with a job: "to dress it and to keep it." Tend it and guard it. And the Psalms add whose it is: "The earth is the LORD's, and the fulness thereof." In that picture, people are gardeners and keepers, not owners. Fourth, heaven under our feet. Henry David Thoreau, in Walden, writing about a pond in winter, put it this way: "Heaven is under our feet as well as over our heads." He wasn't a monk or a saint, but he arrived at a similar place: the ground is holy ground. Sister earth isn't an abstraction. It's the strip of grass by the bus stop, the window box, the park with the litter in it. Love for the earth starts with one patch of it.
screen: `BROTHER SUN, SISTER WATER.` · `OUR SISTER, MOTHER EARTH.` · `TO DRESS IT AND TO KEEP IT.` · `HEAVEN UNDER OUR FEET.` · then, large: `SISTER EARTH.`

segments.voice: Put your feet flat on the floor, and feel the weight of your body settle down through them. Somewhere below the floor, below the building, is soil. Rest your attention there for a few breaths. Then let one patch of ground come to mind that you pass often: a tree pit, a yard, a roadside verge, a park bench. See it clearly, litter and all. Ask what one small act of keeping it would look like. If you pray, you can give thanks to God for the earth beneath you. The bell holds the time.
The earth. The ground that Francis called our sister and our mother, that Genesis gives people to dress and keep, and that Thoreau found heaven in. Today's word.
Your line: sister earth. Today, care for one patch of ground: pick up the litter on it, water it, or plant something in it. Day eight hundred sixty-six.

howItsDone: Christians sing and pray Francis's Canticle of the Creatures, and some churches and communities hold creation-care days, garden work and cleanups; Jews and Christians read Genesis 2 as a call to tend and keep the earth.

trapdoor: what you thought: the earth is scenery, or a resource.
what it means: in Francis's song she's family, both sister and mother.
what a scholar hears: Francis's Canticle uses family names for each creature, and Genesis 2 frames the human role as dressing and keeping the garden.

notes: Audit pass: cut 'the ground he's lying on', an invented detail not in the sources.

The Canticle is paraphrased throughout (sun beautiful and radiant; water useful, humble, precious and pure; earth who sustains and governs us and brings forth fruits with colored flowers and herbs); no translation is quoted. Confirm against a standard edition.

Editor pass: fixed the garbled hook sentence that repeated 'his eyes were failing'; replaced 'calling something your sister changes what you're allowed to do to it', which echoed day 865's closing line about the word sister, with a line about kin rather than owner; changed 'we're made of the same stuff' (not in the Canticle) to 'kin, alongside us'.
'Tradition says he made it late in his life, when he was sick and his eyes were failing' is framed as tradition; confirm the framing.
Thoreau: confirm the quotation is from 'The Pond in Winter' in Walden.
Genesis 2:15 says 'the man' in the KJV; the script says 'the first human'. Confirm acceptable.
The fork's 'a garden that's not yours' reflects the Psalm 24 framing (the earth is the LORD's), not Genesis 2 alone.
